 Running Proxmox on a NAS gives you hot-swap drive bays for bulk storage and a Type 1 hypervisor for VMs, containers, and passthrough in one compact, low-power box. Not every NAS can do it. The difference comes down to four things: firmware access, CPU virtualization extensions, memory capacity, and Linux driver support for the onboard network ports.
 Most NAS units are designed to run one proprietary operating system. Synology supports only DSM on its hardware. Warranty terms vary too: TerraMaster’s FAQ says installing another operating system voids the warranty. And most NAS units ship with 4 to 8 GB of RAM, which is enough for the stock OS but not for a hypervisor running several VMs.
 This guide covers three x86 NAS models that owners run bare-metal Proxmox on, explains why Synology doesn’t fit, and shows when a mini PC is the smarter choice. Proxmox VE 9, built on Debian 13, is the current release. Version 8 reached end of life on August 31, 2026, so install 9 on a new build.
 Our Pick: TerraMaster F4-424 Pro
 The TerraMaster F4-424 Pro is the most capable Proxmox host here: 32 GB of DDR5, an 8-core i3-N305 with VT-x and VT-d, and HDMI output for firmware access.
 CPU: Intel Core i3-N305, 8 cores and 8 threads, up to 3.8 GHz, with VT-x and VT-d (Intel)
 Memory: 32 GB DDR5 on one SODIMM, which TerraMaster lists as the maximum
 Storage: 4x SATA bays + 2x M.2 NVMe (PCIe 3.0 x1)
 Network and video: 2x 2.5GbE, HDMI 2.0b
 Rated power: 13W with drives hibernating and 33W during read/write (TerraMaster)
 Before you wipe TOS, know the warranty position. TerraMaster’s FAQ says its NAS units are built for TOS and that installing another operating system voids the warranty and ends technical support. Owners still run Proxmox on the 424 series, and community install guides are easy to find, but you do it at your own risk.
 Firmware and Boot Process
 Connect a monitor to the HDMI port, plug in a USB keyboard, and enter the firmware setup during boot to set the boot order and confirm that virtualization is enabled. Write the Proxmox ISO to a USB drive, boot from it, and install to one of the M.2 SSDs.
 CPU and Virtualization
 The i3-N305’s eight efficiency cores give you real headroom for several VMs. A typical layout: a TrueNAS VM for storage management (2 cores, 8 GB), a Docker LXC for your self-hosted stack (2 cores, 8 GB), a Home Assistant OS VM (2 cores, 2 GB), and a Windows VM for occasional use (2 cores, 8 GB). That leaves room for the host and a little spare. The same plan does not fit on a quad-core with 16 GB.
 VT-x (hardware virtualization) and VT-d (directed I/O for passthrough) let you pass a USB controller, a NIC, or, with caveats, the SATA controller directly to a VM. Onboard devices may share an IOMMU group with the SATA controller, which can complicate clean passthrough; see the passthrough options below.
 One quirk worth knowing: Intel lists 16 GB as the official memory maximum for the i3-N305, but TerraMaster ships and supports 32 GB in this model.
 Network and Drivers
 The Proxmox installer includes the mainline Linux drivers for common 2.5GbE chips, so the ports usually work without extra downloads. TerraMaster’s spec sheet doesn’t name the network controller, so boot a Linux live USB and run lspci before committing. Intel i225 and i226 chips use the in-kernel igc driver, the lowest-risk option under Proxmox. Realtek RTL8125 chips use r8169, which works but has a more mixed track record in home-lab setups.
 With two ports, you can bond them for redundancy or split management and VM traffic during setup.
 Storage for Proxmox
 Install Proxmox to one of the two M.2 SSDs to keep the OS off your data drives, and use the second M.2 for VM disks. The four SATA bays handle bulk storage in a ZFS pool managed by Proxmox, or passed through to a TrueNAS VM. A common layout: Proxmox on a 256 GB NVMe, a second NVMe for VM disks, and four hard drives in RAIDZ1 for data.
 SATA controller passthrough to a TrueNAS VM depends on IOMMU grouping on your unit. If the controller shares a group with other devices, use disk passthrough or let Proxmox manage the ZFS pool instead. Test before you commit to that architecture.
 The Trade-offs
 32 GB is the official ceiling. It is comfortable for a single node running three to five VMs and containers, but a hypervisor with eight or more VMs will hit it. There’s no PCIe slot, so no 10GbE card, no HBA for more drives, and no add-in GPU. And the warranty caveat above applies to every Proxmox install on this unit.
 If you’re already running Docker on a NAS and want to move up to Proxmox, see our best NAS for Docker guide, where the F4-424 Pro is also the top pick.
 Best Value: QNAP TS-464
 The QNAP TS-464 is a Proxmox-capable NAS with the only PCIe expansion slot in this guide. It has half the cores and half the memory ceiling of the TerraMaster, but for a two- or three-VM setup it delivers what matters: firmware access over HDMI, VT-d, and expansion.
 CPU: Intel Celeron N5095, 4 cores and 4 threads, up to 2.9 GHz, with VT-x and VT-d (Intel)
 Memory: 8 GB DDR4 in two SODIMM slots, 16 GB maximum (QNAP)
 Storage: 4x SATA bays + 2x M.2 NVMe (PCIe 3.0 x1)
 Network and video: 2x 2.5GbE, one PCIe Gen 3 x2 slot, HDMI 2.1
 Rated power: 21.6W in sleep and 40.5W in typical operation with all bays populated (QNAP)
 Firmware Access and Boot
 Connect HDMI and a USB keyboard, enter the firmware setup at boot, and set your Proxmox SSD as the first boot device. QTS lives on the TS-464’s 4 GB internal flash, which QNAP describes as dual-boot OS protection. Install Proxmox to an M.2 SSD and leave that flash alone so you keep a path back to QTS. Check the boot order after firmware updates or a power loss.
 CPU and Virtualization
 The N5095 has four cores, four threads, VT-x, and VT-d. It handles Proxmox plus two or three light guests: a Docker LXC (1 to 2 cores, 4 to 6 GB), a Pi-hole or DNS container (1 core, 512 MB), and a small utility VM. It isn’t a good fit for a Windows VM alongside a busy Linux stack.
 The PCIe Gen 3 x2 slot is where the TS-464 pulls ahead. Install a 10GbE NIC and pass it to a VM, or add a SATA HBA for clean controller passthrough to a TrueNAS VM. No other NAS in this guide has a PCIe slot.
 Network and Drivers
 As with the TerraMaster, QNAP’s spec sheet doesn’t name the onboard 2.5GbE controller, so confirm it with lspci from a live USB. The PCIe slot also lets you add a dedicated NIC for VM traffic, separate from the two onboard ports.
 Storage Considerations
 Install Proxmox to an M.2 NVMe, use the second M.2 for VM storage, and put the four SATA bays into a ZFS pool managed by Proxmox, or pass them to a TrueNAS VM. If onboard SATA passthrough is messy, an HBA in the PCIe slot gives a TrueNAS VM clean access to its own controller.
 The Trade-offs
 QNAP lists 16 GB as the official memory ceiling across two DDR4 SODIMM slots, and Proxmox uses part of that itself, so this stays a light-virtualization platform. QNAP won’t support Proxmox, so keep QTS’s flash intact and document how to boot back to it before you depend on the new setup.
 For more on the TS-464 beyond Proxmox, see our best 4-bay NAS roundup.
 Budget Pick: ASUSTOR AS5402T
 The ASUSTOR AS5402T is the least expensive way into Proxmox on a NAS in this guide. It uses an Intel N5105, a close relative of the TS-464’s N5095, plus four M.2 NVMe slots that make an interesting all-flash VM layout. The two-bay limit keeps it in budget or lab territory.
 CPU: Intel Celeron N5105, 4 cores and 4 threads, up to 2.9 GHz, with VT-x and VT-d (Intel)
 Memory: 4 GB DDR4 in two slots, 16 GB maximum (ASUSTOR)
 Storage: 2x SATA bays + 4x M.2 NVMe (PCIe 3.0 x1)
 Network and video: 2x 2.5GbE, HDMI 2.0b
 Rated power: 12.7W with disks hibernating and 22.9W in operation (ASUSTOR)
 Firmware Access and Boot
 HDMI output and a USB keyboard get you into the firmware setup, where you set the boot order and enable virtualization. Write the Proxmox ISO to USB, boot it, and install to one of the four M.2 slots. As with the other two, confirm the network controller with lspci from a live USB first.
 The All-Flash Angle
 Four M.2 NVMe slots in a two-bay NAS is unusual, and it makes an interesting Proxmox layout: Proxmox on one NVMe, a ZFS mirror on two more for VM storage, and the fourth as a fast scratch pool. The two SATA bays hold bulk data on hard drives. Each M.2 slot is PCIe 3.0 x1, so the gain is latency and IOPS rather than per-drive sequential speed.
 Known Issues
 Fan and LED control outside ADM. Without ADM, the fans and front-panel LEDs need the community asustor-platform-driver, which lists the AS5402T among its supported models and adds fan control through an extra IT87 hardware-monitoring module. Plan to build and maintain it yourself.
 4 GB of RAM is too little. Plan to upgrade toward the 16 GB maximum right away; Proxmox with even one VM on 4 GB will swap.
 ASUSTOR doesn’t support Proxmox. Expect no help from ASUSTOR support, and check your warranty terms before replacing ADM.
 The Trade-offs
 Two hard-drive bays limit bulk storage to a single mirror or two separate drives. The 16 GB ceiling matches the QNAP, and the N5105 gives you about the same two- or three-VM capacity. With no PCIe slot, there’s no expansion path for 10GbE or an HBA. But for a small Proxmox node with all-flash VM storage, it’s an inexpensive way in.
 Why Not Synology for Proxmox?
 Synology is one of the most recommended NAS brands for good reason: DSM is excellent, the app ecosystem is mature, and reliability is strong. For Proxmox, though, Synology is a non-starter.
 DSM only. Synology designs its hardware to run DSM and provides no supported way to boot another operating system.
 No video output. Current Plus models such as the DS925+ have no HDMI port, so there’s no display for a firmware setup screen or an installer.
 The alternative is Synology VMM. Synology’s Virtual Machine Manager runs KVM-based VMs on top of DSM. It works for one or two light VMs on a model with enough memory (the DS925+ takes up to 32 GB of ECC memory), but it’s a DSM package, not a bare-metal hypervisor, and it doesn’t offer Proxmox’s LXC containers or tooling.
 If you want a Synology for NAS duties and Proxmox for virtualization, the right architecture is a separate Proxmox server (a mini PC or other dedicated hardware) mounting Synology shares over NFS or iSCSI. See our TerraMaster vs. Synology comparison for more on the NAS OS trade-offs.
 When a Mini PC Is Better Than a NAS for Proxmox
 A NAS chassis makes sense for Proxmox when you need hot-swap drive bays and want to consolidate storage and compute in one box. For pure virtualization, a mini PC often wins. Here’s when to skip the NAS:
 You need more than 32 GB of RAM. The F4-424 Pro tops out at 32 GB. Intel lists 16 GB as the official maximum for N-series chips like the N100 and i3-N305, even though some vendors ship 32 GB. For 64 GB or more, you need a mini PC with a higher-end processor and two SO-DIMM slots.
 You need PCIe passthrough flexibility. The NAS units here have at most one small PCIe slot. Most mini PCs have none either, so for a GPU, a 10GbE NIC, and an HBA at once, you need a small tower or a workstation-class mini PC with a PCIe slot.
 You don’t need four or more drive bays. If your VMs run from NVMe and bulk data lives on a separate NAS, a mini PC with one or two M.2 slots is simpler, and you aren’t paying for bays you won’t use.
 You want standard firmware and documentation. Mini PCs are ordinary PCs. There’s no internal OS flash to preserve, no NAS fan controller to work around, and no vendor warranty clause about replacing the NAS OS.
 For mini PC recommendations, see our best mini PC for Proxmox guide. The ideal setup for many home labs is a Proxmox mini PC for compute and a NAS for storage, connected over 2.5GbE or 10GbE with NFS.
 How to Choose: Buying Criteria
 Firmware Accessibility
 This is the first gate. If you can’t reach the firmware setup to change the boot order and enable VT-d, Proxmox is dead in the water. All three NAS units in this guide have HDMI output, so you can reach their setup screens with a monitor and a USB keyboard. Synology offers no equivalent. Before buying any NAS for Proxmox, search for “[model name] Proxmox install” and confirm that owners have done it.
 CPU Virtualization Extensions (VT-x and VT-d)
 VT-x is Intel’s hardware virtualization extension, and all three CPUs here support it. Without it, Proxmox can’t run hardware-accelerated VMs.
 VT-d (Intel Virtualization Technology for Directed I/O) enables PCIe passthrough: handing a physical device (NIC, USB controller, SATA controller, GPU) directly to a VM with near-native performance. VT-d is essential for:
 Passing the SATA controller to a TrueNAS VM for direct disk access
 Passing a 10GbE NIC to a specific VM
 Passing a USB controller to a Home Assistant VM for Zigbee or Z-Wave sticks
 Intel lists VT-d for the i3-N305, N5095, and N5105. Check that it’s enabled in the firmware setup, since some systems ship with it off.
 RAM: More Than You Think
 Proxmox allocates memory to each VM. Ballooning and overcommit exist, but plan as if every VM needs its full allocation.
 Component RAM Needed 
 Proxmox host OS 1-2 GB 
 TrueNAS VM (storage) 8 GB minimum (TrueNAS guidance) 
 Docker LXC container 2-8 GB (depends on stack size) 
 Home Assistant OS VM 2 GB 
 Ubuntu/Debian utility VM 1-4 GB 
 Windows 10/11 VM 4-8 GB 
 On 16 GB, you can run Proxmox plus two or three small VMs with little headroom. On 32 GB, you get Proxmox, a TrueNAS VM, a Docker LXC, and two or three more VMs comfortably. That’s why the TerraMaster’s 32 GB matters: the QNAP and ASUSTOR both max out at 16 GB, which limits them to a starter setup.
 Network Controllers: Intel vs. Realtek
 Proxmox VE 9 runs on Debian 13 with its own Linux kernel (6.14 at the 9.0 release). Intel’s i225 and i226 2.5GbE chips use the in-kernel igc driver and work out of the box with the Proxmox installer. Realtek’s RTL8125 uses the r8169 driver. It works, but it has a more mixed record under sustained VM traffic, and some owners switch to Realtek’s out-of-tree r8125 driver. If you’re choosing between two otherwise identical systems, prefer Intel.
 None of the three vendors here names its network controller on the spec sheet, so confirm it with lspci from a live USB before buying into a plan that depends on it.
 Storage Controller Passthrough
 For users who want to run TrueNAS as a VM managing the physical drives, SATA controller passthrough is the holy grail: it gives TrueNAS direct access to the disks. In practice, NAS SATA controllers often share an IOMMU group with other devices (USB, audio, management controllers), which complicates clean passthrough.
 Options when passthrough is blocked:
 ACS override patch: forces IOMMU group separation. It works, but it weakens the isolation between devices.
 Disk passthrough: pass individual disks (not the controller) to the VM with virtio-scsi. ZFS works fine, but the VM can’t read SMART data, so monitor drive health on the Proxmox host.
 Proxmox-managed ZFS: skip TrueNAS and let Proxmox manage the drives natively. It’s the simplest option, and Proxmox handles ZFS snapshots and replication itself.
 Bottom Line
 The TerraMaster F4-424 Pro is the best NAS for Proxmox. With 32 GB of DDR5, an 8-core i3-N305 with VT-d, and HDMI for firmware access, it’s ready for Proxmox without a memory upgrade. TerraMaster’s FAQ says installing another OS voids the warranty.
 For a Proxmox NAS with a PCIe slot, the QNAP TS-464 gives you HDMI firmware access, VT-d, and room for a 10GbE card in a four-bay chassis. Upgrade to its 16 GB maximum and expect two or three VMs, enough for a focused setup.
 For the cheapest entry point, the ASUSTOR AS5402T gets you Proxmox-capable hardware with four M.2 NVMe slots for all-flash VM storage. Budget for a memory upgrade and plan to set up the community fan driver yourself.
 Skip Synology for Proxmox, since it has no supported path to another OS. And if virtualization matters more than NAS storage, a mini PC for Proxmox gives you more flexibility for the money. Connect a Proxmox mini PC to a NAS over your network so you can upgrade compute and storage separately.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can you install Proxmox on a NAS? Yes, on x86 NAS models with a reachable firmware setup screen and hardware virtualization (Intel VT-x or AMD-V). TerraMaster, QNAP, and ASUSTOR x86 models with HDMI output can boot the Proxmox installer from USB. Synology provides no supported way to boot another operating system on its NAS hardware. You need an HDMI display and a USB keyboard for the firmware setup and installer.
 How much RAM do I need for Proxmox on a NAS? Proxmox itself uses a gigabyte or two, and each VM needs its own allocation: a basic Linux server VM wants 2 to 4 GB, a Windows VM 4 to 8 GB, and a Docker LXC 2 to 8 GB depending on the stack. With 16 GB you can run Proxmox plus two or three light VMs. With 32 GB you can comfortably run four to six VMs or a mix of VMs and containers.
 Why can't you install Proxmox on a Synology NAS? Synology designs its hardware to run DSM only. Current Plus models such as the DS925+ have no video output, and Synology offers no supported way to boot another OS. If you want Proxmox, choose a TerraMaster, QNAP, or ASUSTOR x86 model, or a mini PC, and use the Synology for storage.
 Is a mini PC better than a NAS for Proxmox? For pure virtualization, often yes. Mini PCs with higher-end processors and two SO-DIMM slots take much more memory than the Intel N-series chips in these NAS units. A NAS makes sense when you also need hot-swap drive bays for bulk storage. See our best mini PC for Proxmox guide for recommendations.
 Does installing Proxmox on a NAS void the warranty? It can. TerraMaster's FAQ says installing another operating system voids the warranty and ends technical support. QNAP and ASUSTOR do not support Proxmox either, so expect no software help. Check your model's warranty terms before wiping the stock OS, and keep a way to restore it.

 This isn’t a generic “best NAS” list. Those exist, and PCMag writes them better than I can. This is for homelab people: you want a box that stores files and runs Docker containers, hosts a VM or two, feeds Plex/Jellyfin transcoding, and talks fast to your Proxmox cluster over NFS or iSCSI. That narrows the field to NAS units with real CPUs, enough RAM headroom, and 2.5GbE or better networking.

 How I picked these
 I started with every NAS on Amazon shipping an x86 CPU, 8GB+ RAM (or an upgrade slot), at least one M.2 NVMe bay, and 2.5GbE networking, then cut anything above $1,300 diskless. ARM-only units are out (most VM images and a chunk of container images won’t run), and so are boxes with soldered, non-upgradable RAM under 8GB.
 What’s left is a short list. I evaluated each on four things: CPU performance per dollar, RAM ceiling, out-of-box networking speed, and whether the OS lets you run Docker and VMs without hacks.  An NVMe slot for apps. Spinning disks are for bulk storage. Container volumes, databases, and VM disks belong on the M.2 slots every pick here includes.

The NVMe slots matter more than the bays for this audience: put your container volumes and app databases on NVMe and let the HDDs be pure bulk storage.  Where it fits: a first NAS, a Plex/Jellyfin box for a small library, or a dedicated backup target for your Proxmox cluster (a cheap NAS doing one job well is a legitimate architecture). Where it doesn’t: heavy VM duty or anything needing more than ~80TB of raw capacity (two bays × 24TB NAS drives, RAID 1). Two bays also means RAID 1 or nothing, so plan your redundancy accordingly.

The trade-off: UGOS is functional and improving, but it’s younger and rougher than Synology’s DSM. If you plan to run your own OS anyway, that doesn’t matter.

 The i3-N305 gives you 8 cores and 8 threads (the strongest CPU here) plus 32GB of DDR5 out of the box . For Docker-heavy workloads that’s the most capable machine in this list: the RAM you actually need is already installed.
 The catch is TOS, TerraMaster’s operating system. It works (Docker support exists) but it’s the weakest software of the three, and TerraMaster had documented security issues in 2022–2023: deadbolt ransomware targeted TOS vulnerabilities, and patches were slow. The community’s fix is well-worn: buy the hardware, flash TrueNAS SCALE or Unraid , and never boot TOS. If that plan appeals to you, this is your box.  The asterisks are real, though. The Ryzen V1500B is a 4-core chip with no integrated GPU, so no hardware transcoding , which rules it out as a Jellyfin box for remote clients. It ships with 4GB of RAM you’ll want to upgrade immediately. And the DS925+ generation restricts storage to Synology’s drive compatibility list, which pushed a chunk of the community toward third-party NAS brands this year. That’s the spec sheet of a small tower server, not an appliance. It can host the whole container stack plus several VMs while serving storage to a Proxmox cluster over 10GbE.

 Drives are the expensive half of a NAS right now. Every new-condition hard drive listing I checked on Oct 23 was from a third-party seller, and the cheapest price per TB was a renewed enterprise drive. Three rules before the table:
 CMR only. SMR drives (plain WD Red, most desktop drives) take far longer to rebuild a RAID array or resilver a ZFS pool, and a slow rebuild is when a second drive fails. Seagate IronWolf and IronWolf Pro, WD Red Plus and Red Pro, and Toshiba N300 are CMR lines.

Four of them in RAID 5 on the DXP4800 Plus give you 36TB usable for about $1,800. For container volumes and VM disks, put an NVMe drive in the M.2 slots and keep the hard drives for bulk storage.
 Also worth knowing
 UGREEN DXP480T Plus (~$999): the all-flash sibling. 4x NVMe bays, no SATA, 10GbE. If your homelab data fits in ~16TB of SSD (and you value silence over raw capacity), it’s a clean option. The lack of SATA bays means no cheap bulk storage, though. Every TB costs flash prices.
 QNAP TS-464: a year ago this was a contender. The Intel N5095 is showing its age against the N305 and Pentium Gold 8505 in the picks above, QNAP’s software has had its own security troubles, and the price hasn’t dropped to match. I’d skip it this cycle.
 Or skip the NAS: mini PC + DAS
 Before buying a NAS at all, price the alternative: an N150 mini PC running Proxmox or plain Docker, plus a USB DAS enclosure for the bulk disks. On Oct 23 that was a Beelink EQ14 at $369 (16GB, dual 2.5GbE; more options in the home server mini PC guide ) and a TerraMaster D4-320 at $170.99 (4 bays over 10Gbps USB-C, 4.2★ from 395 ratings). That’s about $540 diskless, against $657 for the DXP4800 Plus.

 You want a storage appliance 
 You want one Proxmox cluster anyway 
 If you already run a Proxmox mini PC or plan to, a NAS appliance is mostly redundant. Attach storage to the cluster and be done. Buy the NAS when you want storage to be a separate, boring, always-on appliance that survives your cluster experiments.
 One caveat with the DAS route: a USB enclosure puts a USB bridge between the disks and the OS. ZFS and mdadm work on it, but a flaky bridge shows up as disks dropping out of the pool. On day one, check that SMART data comes through ( smartctl -a /dev/sdX ) and leave the pool under load for a few hours before you trust it with data.
 If I were buying today
 Under $400: The DXP2800 . It runs Docker and VMs, the N100 sips power, and you can always add a second NAS later if you outgrow two bays.
 Best overall for homelab: The DXP4800 Plus . 10GbE at $657 is a hardware gap nobody else closes, and the 64GB RAM ceiling means you won’t hit a wall.
 Most compute for the money: The F4-424 Pro , but only if you’re flashing your own OS. The i3-N305 + 32GB out of the box is hard to beat if you never plan to touch TOS.
 Best appliance experience: The DS925+ . Accept no transcoding and the drive whitelist, and you get software that genuinely works for five years with minimal attention.
 Money no object, one box: The DXP6800 Pro . i5, dual 10GbE, six bays, TB4. It replaces a small server.
 And whichever you buy, put it on a UPS. A CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD is the $240 insurance that keeps a hard power cut from corrupting your array. If the NAS sits in a rack, the best rack mount UPS guide covers 1U and 2U units. More on that and the rest of the homelab stack in my Black Friday deals tracker and the Docker containers guide .
 FAQ
 What is the best NAS for a homelab in 2026? For most homelabs, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus: $656.99 on Oct 23, 10GbE plus 2.5GbE, 4 bays plus 2 NVMe slots, RAM up to 64GB, and official support for running TrueNAS, Unraid or Proxmox instead of UGOS. Under $400, the DXP2800. If you want the best software and don’t need hardware transcoding, the Synology DS925+.
 Which hard drives should I put in a NAS? CMR NAS drives: Seagate IronWolf or IronWolf Pro, WD Red Plus or Red Pro, Toshiba N300. Avoid SMR drives in any RAID or ZFS pool. On Oct 23 the best new-drive value I found was the Seagate IronWolf 12TB at $449.99 ($37.50 per TB) from a third-party seller. A renewed Exos X24 was cheaper per TB, with a refurbisher warranty instead of Seagate’s.
 Can these NAS units run Docker containers directly? Yes. All three support Docker natively (UGREEN and Synology have container managers in their OS; TerraMaster supports Docker in TOS). For heavier VM workloads, the UGREEN and TerraMaster hardware handles it; the Synology’s 4GB of base RAM needs an upgrade first.
 Do I need 10GbE for a homelab NAS? Not strictly. 2.5GbE saturates HDDs fine (~280MB/s). 10GbE matters when you add NVMe pools, run VM disks over NFS/iSCSI, or have multiple clients hitting the NAS at once. The DXP4800 Plus having it at $657 removes the dilemma.
 What's the Synology drive whitelist issue? The DS925+ generation only supports drives on Synology’s compatibility list, which favors Synology-branded and enterprise drives and excludes many popular WD/Seagate models. It’s the main reason long-time Synology users have been defecting to UGREEN and DIY builds.
 NAS or just a big USB drive on my mini PC? A DAS enclosure on a mini PC is cheaper and simpler for single-server setups. Buy the NAS when you want RAID management, snapshots, and backups handled by software designed for it, or when storage needs to stay up while your compute boxes get experimented on.
 How much RAM do I need for Docker on a NAS? 8GB runs a handful of containers. If you’re adding Immich, a Plex instance, a couple of databases, and maybe a Home Assistant VM, 32GB is where it stops being tight. That’s why the F4-424 Pro shipping with 32GB matters.

 A home-lab NAS has two jobs: protect data and support the services that depend on it. Choose the type of NAS first (two bays or four, hard drives or flash, appliance or DIY, one box or separate compute), then the model. This guide routes each home-lab job to the right kind of NAS, names one current pick per route, and links to the dedicated guide for model-by-model detail.
 Start with the job

 One box for everything: QNAP TS-464
 The TS-464 is our top pick when one appliance has to do most of the work. It combines four SATA bays, two M.2 slots, dual 2.5GbE, Intel graphics that Plex can use for hardware transcoding, and a PCIe slot that QNAP lists for optional 5GbE or 10GbE cards. QNAP lists 8GB on a SODIMM, two SODIMM slots, and a 16GB official maximum, so the memory is upgradeable.
 The operational requirement is disciplined security: patch promptly, disable unnecessary services, and keep the management interface off the open internet. For the other current four-bay options, including the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus with built-in 10GbE and the ASUSTOR AS5404T with four M.2 slots, see our best 4-bay NAS roundup .
 Backup-first storage: Synology DS925+
 The DS925+ is the current four-bay Synology. Its value is DSM: Active Backup, Hyper Backup, snapshots, alerts, accounts, permissions, and recovery documentation. It has dual 2.5GbE and no PCIe slot, so it cannot take Synology’s 10GbE module.
 Since DSM 7.3 (October 2025), Synology’s 2025 Plus, Value and J models, such as the DS925+ and DS225+, accept third-party 3.5-inch HDDs and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs, but M.2 storage pools and cache still need drives on Synology’s compatibility list. Choose the DS925+ when the NAS is primarily trusted storage rather than the fastest application server.
 A compact backup target: two bays
 The DS225+ is the current compact Synology for mirrored storage, household backup, and a modest set of services. It is not a miniature four-bay system: two bays limit capacity planning and expansion. If you see the previous-generation DS224+, compare it on capability and lifecycle, not remaining-stock price. Our best 2-bay NAS guide covers QNAP, TerraMaster, ASUSTOR, and UGREEN alternatives.
 Fast storage for VMs and databases: all-flash
 When the NAS holds VM disks, databases, or container volumes, latency matters more than capacity. The TerraMaster F8 SSD Plus has eight M.2 NVMe slots, a Core i3-N305, and 10GbE in a small chassis. Each slot runs on a single PCIe 3.0 lane, which is plenty for network storage but not a desktop NVMe drive’s full speed. Keep bulk media and backups on hard drives elsewhere, because flash costs far more per terabyte. See our all-flash NAS guide for the alternatives.
 Heavy applications on the NAS: TerraMaster F4-424 Pro
 The F4-424 Pro is the application-heavy choice. The 8-core Core i3-N305 and 32GB of installed memory leave far more room for containers, databases, indexing, and media services than the other four-bays here. It is less compelling as low-maintenance file storage, where DSM’s tooling is worth more than unused compute. Our Docker NAS and Proxmox NAS guides go deeper.
 Full control: a DIY NAS
 A DIY build running TrueNAS Community Edition (formerly TrueNAS SCALE) or Unraid gives you standard PC parts, ZFS or flexible arrays, and no vendor lock-in. The tradeoff is that every update, driver, and recovery step is yours. Our DIY NAS vs Synology guide compares the cost and maintenance, and our NAS OS guide compares the software.
 Compute separate from storage
 Many home labs work best with the NAS as storage and backup and a mini PC for VMs and heavier containers, connected over NFS or SMB on 2.5GbE or faster. That split keeps experiments and upgrades away from the storage appliance. Our mini PC vs NAS guide explains the tradeoff, and our Proxmox mini PC guide covers the compute side.
 Buying criteria
 Recovery comes first
 RAID protects availability after a drive failure. It does not protect against deletion, corruption, ransomware, theft, fire, or a failed enclosure. Maintain at least one independent versioned copy and test a real restore.
 Match network speed to storage
 2.5GbE is enough for many HDD arrays and household workflows. 10GbE matters for large sequential transfers, fast SSD pools, VM storage, and multiple demanding clients.
 Separate storage from experimentation
 A NAS can run containers, but every additional service expands the failure and security surface around important data. Back up application data independently, and consider separate compute when experimentation would make storage maintenance risky.
 Bottom line
 The QNAP TS-464 is our top pick when one NAS has to do most of the work. Choose the Synology DS925+ for software-first backup storage, the DS225+ for a compact mirror, the F8 SSD Plus for all-flash speed, or the F4-424 Pro when containers and applications are the main job.
 Synology lists the DS923+ as discontinued, and the DS224+ is the previous generation. Consider either only for used, clearance, or migration comparisons.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best NAS for most home labs? For a home lab where one NAS stores data and also runs media and containers, the QNAP TS-464. Choose the Synology DS925+ when managed backup and storage that requires little administration matter more than hardware flexibility, the same split our Synology vs QNAP guide makes.
 Do I need four bays? Four bays create more capacity and RAID-layout options. Two bays suit a compact mirrored backup target, but expansion usually means replacing drives or the enclosure.
 Which NAS is best for 10GbE? The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus includes a 10GbE port, the QNAP TS-464 can add 5GbE or 10GbE through its PCIe slot, and the TerraMaster F8 SSD Plus pairs 10GbE with all-flash storage. Our best 4-bay NAS guide compares the four-bay options.
 Should my NAS also be my compute server? Only for a modest service set. A NAS can run containers, but moving heavier compute to a mini PC keeps experiments away from the storage appliance. Our mini PC vs NAS guide covers the split.
 Is the Synology DS923+ still a current recommendation? No. Synology lists it as discontinued. The DS925+ is the current four-bay model; consider a DS923+ only used or at clearance when you need its 10GbE slot.

 On this page 9 sections A good home server build starts with the job, not the parts list. Most people need one of three machines: a small, low-power box for containers and a few services, a mid-range tower that stores your files and runs Plex or Jellyfin and some VMs, or a rack build with hot-swap bays, remote management and 10GbE. This guide covers all three, with one checked example per part and a “buy instead” option for each.
 There are no prices in this guide. RAM and SSD prices moved too fast this year for a quoted number to stay true, so read build, buy or wait during the RAM shortage before you shop. The idle power figures come from ENERGY STAR test data. Where no measured figure exists, we say so.

 Before you build: mini PC, used office PC, NAS or DIY
 Building is not always the right call. Four routes cover nearly everyone:
 Mini PC. Small, quiet and very low power. Limited to one or two internal SSDs and, on N-series chips, 16 GB of RAM. Our best mini PC for a home lab picks models.
 Used 1-liter office PC. A ThinkCentre Tiny, EliteDesk Mini or OptiPlex Micro gets you a full desktop Core chip with more RAM headroom for the cost of a used part. The tradeoffs are covered in mini PC vs used workstation for a home lab .
 Prebuilt NAS. The easiest way to get four or more drive bays with a supported OS. You give up CPU choice and some upgrade room. Start with our NAS setup for beginners .
 DIY. Build when you need things the boxes above don’t offer: more bays, ECC, a full-size GPU, an HBA or 10GbE in one machine.
 Try it in the Lab · NAS · Plex/Jellyfin · Proxmox · game servers · local AI Home Server Configurator Pick your jobs (NAS, Plex, Proxmox, game servers, local AI), your drive count and a budget tier, and get a sourced spec for the CPU, RAM, drives and power. It also flags when a mini PC or used server is the better answer. 
 Starter build: low power for containers and light VMs
 The starter build runs a self-hosting starter stack : a reverse proxy, a password manager, Home Assistant, ad blocking, maybe Immich on a modest library. None of that needs many cores. It needs low idle power, because the box never turns off. For the password manager, our guide for self-hosters covers whether to run Vaultwarden yourself or use a hosted vault.
 Platform: an Intel N-series mini PC, or a used 1-liter PC. Intel’s N150 is the current reference chip for this tier: 4 cores and 4 threads, a 6 W base power rating, Quick Sync video, and VT-x and VT-d for virtualization. Its limits are just as clear on Intel’s spec page: 16 GB of memory maximum, one memory channel, and no ECC. If security cameras are part of the plan, our Home Assistant and Frigate mini PC guide sizes the box by camera count.
 A used 1-liter PC trades a little idle power for a desktop-class chip and more memory slots. ENERGY STAR’s short-idle figures show the spread:

 Storage. One NVMe SSD for the OS and apps, plus a second drive for data if the chassis has room. TrueNAS’s guide warns against USB disks for primary storage, so a mini PC with USB drives hanging off it is not a NAS. When you outgrow internal storage, move to the mid-range build or add a dedicated NAS.

 Mid-range build: NAS, Plex or Jellyfin, and Proxmox in one box
 This is what most people mean by “home server”: a tower with four to eight hard drives, a media server and a few VMs. Our self-hosted home guide covers what runs on it.
 CPU: Quick Sync first, then cores
 For media, the integrated GPU matters more than core count. Plex and Jellyfin both document Intel Quick Sync for hardware transcoding, and Jellyfin’s Intel guide lists which codecs each GPU generation handles. An Intel desktop chip with UHD 770 graphics covers it without a separate card. Our best mini PC for Plex and Jellyfin 4K transcoding guide goes through the generations in detail. If the server will run Jellyfin or Plex, check how many transcodes it can handle before picking a CPU or GPU.
 The Core i5-14500 is our reference chip. Intel’s spec page lists 14 cores (6 performance, 8 efficient) and 20 threads, a 65 W base and 154 W max turbo rating, up to 192 GB of memory, ECC support, and UHD Graphics 770 with Quick Sync. ECC needs a W680 board on top of that.
 AMD’s Ryzen 9 9900X is the many-cores option at 12 cores and 24 threads. AMD lists ECC support as dependent on the motherboard. It has no Quick Sync, so transcoding goes to the CPU or an added GPU.
 Low power or more cores? For a box that idles most of the day and serves files and streams, pick the chip with Quick Sync and enough cores for your VMs. Go for more cores only when you know you’ll run sustained workloads like many VMs, compiling code or game servers.
 Mid-range CPU

 RAM: size for ZFS, VMs and apps separately
 Plan RAM in layers:
 Storage (ZFS). TrueNAS’s hardware guide asks for 8 GB for basic operation with up to eight drives, plus 1 GB per drive after the eighth. Proxmox’s requirements put ZFS at about 1 GB per TB of used storage on top of the host.
 Host. Proxmox wants at least 2 GB for the OS itself.
 Guests. Add every VM’s allocation. TrueNAS suggests 16 GB as good and 32 GB or more as optimal for iSCSI and VM workloads.
 Add those up and most mid-range builds land at 32 GB, with 64 GB if you run several VMs or a large pool. Skip dedup unless you have a specific reason. TrueNAS budgets 5 GB of RAM per TB of deduplicated data.
 Do you need ECC for ZFS? TrueNAS’s own wording: most users strongly recommend ECC, and many TrueNAS systems run every day without it. If your board and CPU support it, buy it; don’t skip ZFS because you can’t.
 Case, bays and drives
 Count the drives you want in three years, not today. Plan the RAIDZ layout up front: the OpenZFS RAIDZ documentation says the minimum number of devices in a raidz group is one more than the number of parity disks, and “the recommended number is between 3 and 9 to help increase performance.”
 The Fractal Design Node 804 is a common micro-ATX choice. Fractal lists up to 8 3.5-inch and 4 2.5-inch drives, or up to 10 3.5-inch and 2 2.5-inch, in a dual-chamber layout.
 For drives, use CMR, not SMR. TrueNAS’s guide says to avoid SMR drives in ZFS pools. Western Digital’s WD Red Plus line is CMR and rated for NAS systems up to 8 bays. TrueNAS also advises against USB boot drives, so boot from a small SSD.

 Rack build: hot-swap bays, IPMI, HBA and 10GbE
 The rack build is for people who outgrow a tower. It makes sense once you want more than about 10 drives, hot-swap trays, remote management, or a network faster than 2.5GbE.
 Chassis size and rack depth
 Depth is the spec that catches people. The SilverStone RM43-320-RS, a 4U chassis with 20 hot-swap 3.5-inch bays, is 660 mm deep, and its included rails need a rack with 663 to 915 mm between front and rear mounting holes. Many wall-mount and short network racks are shallower than that. Measure your rack’s usable depth before you buy, and read our home networking hub for where the switch, patch panel and UPS go.
 4U chassis fit full-height cards and quieter 120 mm fans. Both matter at home. The RM43-320-RS ships with three 120 mm hot-swap fans and takes a standard ATX power supply.

 IPMI. TrueNAS lists the benefits as remote power control, a remote console and virtual media, so you can reinstall the OS without walking to the rack. One example: Supermicro’s X13SAE-F is an ATX board for 12th to 14th gen Core chips with the W680 chipset, up to 192 GB of ECC or non-ECC DDR5, an AST2600 management controller with a dedicated IPMI port, and 8 SATA ports. Pair it with the i5-14500 and you have ECC, Quick Sync and remote management on one board.
 HBA in IT mode. A 20-bay backplane needs more ports than any board has. TrueNAS recommends HBAs such as LSI 9211 or SAS2008-class cards, including the IBM M1015 and Dell H200 flashed to IT mode, and says not to use hardware RAID, because ZFS needs direct disk access. Proxmox makes the same point: ZFS is not compatible with hardware RAID controllers. Check that your HBA and cables match the backplane’s connector.
 10GbE. TrueNAS’s guide favors Intel and Chelsio NICs, recommends one faster link over bonding several slow ones, and points to SFP+ for 10Gb. You also need a switch with SFP+ ports, which our home network setup guide helps you plan.
 Virtualizing TrueNAS? TrueNAS does not support running on virtual disks in production. If you run it under Proxmox, pass through the HBA, which needs VT-d (AMD-Vi on AMD). If you have not settled on a NAS OS yet, our TrueNAS vs Unraid comparison covers the trade-offs.
 Buy instead: A used enterprise server is often the cheaper way into this tier. Our best used server for a home lab compares Dell, HPE and Lenovo models by idle power and noise, and the Home Server Configurator covers used rack and tower servers with their ENERGY STAR idle figures. If the rack is for local AI, read our budget AI server build for GPU hosts and power cabling.
 Power, noise and running cost
 Idle power is the number that costs you money, because a home server spends most of its life idle. The math is simple:
 Yearly kWh = idle watts × 24 × 365 ÷ 1,000. Multiply by your electricity rate from your bill.
 So the 3.4 W NUC uses about 30 kWh a year at idle. The Lenovo ThinkSystem ST50 V3 tower server, at 40.2 W SERT idle in ENERGY STAR’s typical configuration (Xeon E-2456, 32 GB), uses about 352 kWh. The HPE ProLiant ML30 Gen10 Plus (Xeon E-2336, 32 GB) measured 31.3 W, and the 1U HPE DL20 Gen10 Plus measured 36.8 W. All are before you add hard drives.
 Yearly kWh at idle from the measured idle figures above. Original Sillectus chart. 
 For DIY mid-range and rack builds, no measured idle figure is published, because every build is different. Measure yours with a plug-in meter after setup, then run the numbers.
 Try it in the Lab · Watts → dollars → minutes on battery Homelab Power Cost + UPS Runtime Calculator Enter idle and load watts, hours under load and your electricity rate to get a monthly and yearly cost. 
 Size the power supply from the parts list with the PSU estimator , not from the biggest number on the shelf. On noise, we have no measured figures for these builds, so we won’t quote any. In general, larger, slower fans and a 4U chassis are quieter than 1U and 2U servers.
 A UPS gives ZFS time to shut down cleanly. TrueNAS recommends one, and our guide to keeping your home network running in a power outage covers sizing.
 Plan the drives and the UPS before you order
 Two decisions are cheaper to make on paper than after the parts arrive: how many drives you need for the space you want, and what UPS keeps the box safe in an outage.
 Step 1: work out usable space, not raw space
 Redundancy costs drives, and how much depends on the layout. Six matched 12 TB drives give 72 TB raw, but about 48 TB usable as a TrueNAS RAIDZ2 pool or an Unraid array with dual parity, both of which survive two drive failures. The same six drives as three mirrors give 36 TB. These are TB before file system overhead; our TrueNAS vs Unraid worked example shows the calculation and what changes with mixed drive sizes. Not sure between mirrors and RAIDZ2? See ZFS RAID levels explained for a home NAS.

 Count bays for the layout you pick, plus room to grow. If the case only takes four drives, a six-wide RAIDZ2 is off the table before you start.
 Try it in the Lab · Storage planning for NAS builders ZFS & RAID Capacity Calculator Enter drive count, size and layout to see usable TB and TiB, how many drives can fail, and the ZFS slop reserve. 
 Step 2: size the UPS from watts, then check runtime
 The UPS only has to carry the server long enough to shut down cleanly. Size it against its watt rating, not the larger VA number, and keep your load under about 80 percent of that rating for startup surges. Pick a model with a USB or network port so the server can be told to shut down: NAS systems usually include a UPS client in their settings, and Proxmox hosts commonly use NUT or apcupsd. Our power outage guide covers the shutdown setup step by step. Once you know your server’s idle watts, size a UPS for it with the load at or under 80 percent of the watt rating.
 Use the measured idle figure for your machine (or your plug-in meter reading) plus the drives, add the network gear that shares the UPS, and check the runtime:
 Try it in the Lab · How long will the battery last? UPS Runtime Calculator Sum your devices' watts, enter the UPS battery and efficiency, and see estimated runtime and the load as a share of the UPS rating. 
 Six 4 TB drives in RAIDZ2 give 16 TB usable and survive two failures. Plan the pool here before you order drives. Try the ZFS RAID calculator → 
 Software: Proxmox, TrueNAS, Unraid or Ubuntu with Docker
 Proxmox VE if VMs and containers come first. It needs Intel VT or AMD-V. Run TrueNAS inside it with a passed-through controller if you also want a NAS. See our Proxmox home lab setup guide .
 TrueNAS if storage comes first. It’s ZFS-native with apps on top. Minimums are any x86_64 CPU, 8 GB of RAM, a 20 GB SSD boot device and at least two identical drives per pool. If you plan to run TrueNAS, note the 26-to-27 rename and the advice to wait for 27.0.
 Unraid if you want to mix drive sizes in a parity-protected array and run Docker and VMs. It’s a paid, perpetual license. On October 2, 2026, Unraid’s pricing page listed a Starter tier for up to 6 storage devices and higher tiers with no device limit, plus a 30-day free trial.
 Ubuntu Server with Docker if you are comfortable on the command line and only need containers. It’s the lightest option for the starter build.
 Free Lab tool · NAS · Plex/Jellyfin · Proxmox · game servers · local AI
 Home Server Configurator
 The starter, mid-range and rack builds above are starting points. To match one to your own mix of NAS, Plex or Jellyfin, Proxmox and containers, give the configurator your workloads, budget, noise limit and form factor.
 Configure your build → 
 Frequently asked questions
 How much does it cost to build a home server?
 Price your build by job, not by a headline number. List the platform (mini PC, CPU plus board, or used server), RAM sized for ZFS and your VMs, the drives for your pool plus one spare, a case and power supply, and a UPS. Then check current prices on the day, because RAM and SSD prices moved sharply in 2026. Add the running cost: idle watts × 24 × 365 ÷ 1,000 gives kWh per year.
 How much RAM do I need for a home server?
 16 GB is enough for a container-only starter box, and it is the maximum on Intel N-series chips. For a NAS with Proxmox, plan 32 GB, or 64 GB if you run several VMs. TrueNAS asks for 8 GB for up to eight drives plus 1 GB per extra drive. Proxmox adds about 1 GB per TB of used ZFS storage, plus 2 GB for the host and whatever your guests use.
 What is the best CPU for a home server: low power or more cores?
 For most home servers, low power with Quick Sync. The box idles most of the day, and Intel's integrated graphics handle Plex and Jellyfin transcoding. An N150-class chip covers a starter server. An i5-14500 (14 cores, UHD 770) covers NAS, media and several VMs. Buy many cores, like a 12-core Ryzen 9 9900X, only for sustained workloads.
 Can I build a home server from an old PC?
 Yes, if it has a 64-bit CPU with virtualization support and enough SATA ports for your drives. TrueNAS runs on any x86_64 CPU with 8 GB of RAM, and Proxmox needs Intel VT or AMD-V. Check its idle draw with a plug-in meter first, because an old gaming PC can cost more to run than a new mini PC.
 Should I build a DIY server or buy a NAS?
 Buy a NAS if you mainly need file storage and backups and want a supported, low-effort box. Build if you want Quick Sync transcoding, several VMs, ECC, more than eight drives, an HBA or 10GbE in one machine.
 Do I need ECC memory for ZFS?
 It's recommended, not required. TrueNAS says most users strongly recommend ECC, and that many TrueNAS systems run every day without it. If your CPU and board support ECC, such as an Intel Core chip on a W680 board, use it.
 How many drives should I buy for a home server?
 Decide the layout first. Six matched 12 TB drives give about 48 TB usable as RAIDZ2 or Unraid dual parity, surviving two failures, versus 72 TB raw. Our ZFS and RAID capacity calculator shows usable space for any drive count.
 What size UPS do I need for a home server?
 Size it on the watt rating, not VA, and keep the load under about 80 percent of it. Choose a model with USB or network monitoring so the server shuts down cleanly, and check runtime with our UPS runtime calculator.
 The takeaway
 Match the build to the job. A 3.4 W mini PC covers containers. A Quick Sync i5 with 32 to 64 GB and CMR drives covers a NAS, media and Proxmox box. The rack build only pays off once you need hot-swap bays, IPMI and 10GbE. Size RAM from the TrueNAS and Proxmox rules, buy CMR drives, and measure idle power before you trust any running-cost estimate.

 How to build the perfect homelab setup depends on your workloads, budget, noise tolerance, power limit, storage needs, and recovery time—not on owning the most servers. For most people in 2026, the best design is a quiet, efficient virtualization host, separate backup or NAS storage when needed, segmented networking, private remote access, UPS protection, and tested recovery.
 A homelab should help you learn, self-host services, develop software, practice networking, or store data without becoming an expensive appliance that is difficult to operate. The design below starts with a single efficient machine and expands only when a specific workload justifies additional hardware.

 A single modern desktop or mini PC can run Linux, Docker, Home Assistant, media services, development tools, and several lightweight virtual machines. Add a separate NAS when drive redundancy, snapshots, storage capacity, or backup isolation matters more than having the simplest possible system.
 Key takeaways 
 The best homelab is sized around workloads and recovery requirements, not maximum server count.
 A 16–32 GB mini PC is enough for a starter lab; 32–64 GB is a sensible range for a more serious general-purpose host.
 Docker inside a dedicated Linux VM is the strongest default for a Proxmox-based lab because the application layer remains portable and isolated from the hypervisor.
 ZFS mirrors or RAIDZ can provide disk-failure tolerance, but snapshots and RAID are not backups.
 A managed switch, VLANs, private VPN, MFA, UPS, monitoring, and restore testing matter more than buying 10GbE or rack hardware early.
 Virtualizing the firewall or NAS increases flexibility but also increases the number of systems that can cause an outage.
 What should a perfect homelab setup do? 
 A perfect homelab setup should make experimentation safe, routine services dependable, and recovery understandable. “Perfect” does not mean the fastest CPU, the largest ZFS pool, or a three-node cluster. A quiet, power-efficient, documented system that you can restore after a failed disk or corrupted update is usually more valuable than a powerful rack server that is too loud or expensive to run.

 Do I need a rack server to build a homelab?

 Should OPNsense run in a virtual machine?
 OPNsense can run in a VM, but a dedicated firewall appliance is safer when household internet cannot depend on an experimental homelab. A virtual firewall is best introduced after you have alternate management access, an exported configuration, and a spare router or documented recovery plan.
 Can Tailscale replace application security?
 No. Tailscale can reduce public exposure and provide private access without router port forwarding, but applications still need strong authentication, MFA where available, patching, access controls, and secure credentials.
 The Bottom Line 
 The perfect homelab setup is a system you can afford to run, understand when it fails, and restore without guesswork. Begin with one quiet virtualization host, a dedicated Linux VM for Docker, sensible network segmentation, private remote access, independent backups, and UPS protection. Add a NAS, faster networking, a second host, or rack hardware only when a measured workload or learning objective requires it.

Can You Use Proxmox as a NAS? What Works and What Does Not (2026) 
 Independent Australian Storage & Infrastructure Authority

 Jump to section 
 Proxmox VE can serve NAS storage, but it takes deliberate configuration. Unlike Unraid or TrueNAS, Proxmox assumes no default NAS role. There is no SMB sharing wizard or NAS-style drive health dashboard, although the Proxmox Disks view can display per-disk SMART values. What Proxmox does have is a flexible ZFS implementation, LXC container support, and a Samba package available through apt that you install and configure yourself. If your primary goal is NAS storage, TrueNAS or Unraid is the better starting point. If your primary goal is running VMs and you want storage attached to the same box, Proxmox is worth understanding.
 ⓘ 
 In short: Proxmox can share storage over SMB or NFS but requires manual configuration. One approach is running TrueNAS Community Edition as a VM inside Proxmox with direct disk or storage-controller passthrough. TrueNAS documentation says virtualized TrueNAS is intended for development or ad hoc proof-of-concept use and is not a supported configuration for regular production or critical data. A single Proxmox server can serve both hypervisor and NAS roles with the right setup.
 What Proxmox Is Designed For
 Proxmox Virtual Environment (VE) is an open source hypervisor platform. Its job is managing virtual machines (KVM) and containers (LXC) with enterprise features: live migration, high availability clustering, web-based management, and Proxmox Backup Server integration. Every design decision in Proxmox is oriented toward these workloads.
 Proxmox stores its VM and container images in one of several storage backends: ZFS datasets, LVM volumes, directories, or network storage (NFS, iSCSI, Ceph). All of these are configured through the Proxmox web UI or CLI. Proxmox does not care which you use, as long as the storage backend can serve VM images.
 The gap is NAS-specific management. Proxmox has no concept of a shared folder, no SMB share UI, no drive spin-down, no storage pool health display oriented toward NAS workloads, and no pre-installed SMART monitoring dashboard. These features exist in Unraid and TrueNAS because they were designed for home NAS use. Proxmox was designed for a different audience.
 Three Ways to Run NAS Storage on Proxmox
 Option 1: ZFS Dataset Shared via Samba on Proxmox Directly
 Proxmox supports ZFS natively and can create ZFS pools directly on attached drives from the Proxmox installer or post-install via the CLI. Once a ZFS pool exists, you create filesystem datasets, install Samba via apt, configure smb.conf, and create SMB shares that point to paths in those datasets.
 This approach works and is efficient: no VM overhead, ZFS checksums apply to all data, and Proxmox manages the drives directly. The trade-off is management. Samba share and permission changes require manual Samba/Linux administration, while Proxmox's web UI can handle some disk and ZFS pool operations. There is no web UI for this. If you are comfortable with Linux administration, this is viable. If you want a web interface for day-to-day storage management, it is not the right approach.
 Option 2: TrueNAS Scale Virtualised Inside Proxmox with Disk Passthrough
 Drives are passed directly from the host to the TrueNAS VM using PCIe passthrough of the storage controller (HBA) rather than Proxmox's virtual disk layer. TrueNAS then sees the drives directly and manages them with ZFS as if it were running on bare metal.
 This combination gives you the best of both platforms: Proxmox's superior VM management for workloads like Windows VMs, game servers, and development environments; and TrueNAS's full ZFS stack with its web GUI, scrub scheduling, snapshot management, and replication for data storage.
 This setup requires VT-d or AMD-Vi for passthrough and enough RAM for the host and guests. TrueNAS recommends passing physical disks or the entire storage controller where possible and requires at least 8GB RAM for the TrueNAS VM; total host RAM depends on the storage and guest workloads.
 Option 3: TrueNAS Scale in an LXC Container
 Running TrueNAS in an LXC container instead of a full VM reduces overhead compared to a KVM VM. TrueNAS documents virtualized installation in a full virtual machine and does not provide a Proxmox LXC installation procedure. This approach exists in community documentation but is not recommended for data you care about. Use a KVM VM for TrueNAS if you are virtualising it in Proxmox.
 What You Give Up Compared to a Dedicated NAS OS
 Still deciding? 
 Recommended: Beelink Mini S12 . 
 Check price → 
 Running NAS workloads on Proxmox, whether directly or via a TrueNAS VM, involves trade-offs compared to running TrueNAS or Unraid on bare metal:
 Drive health monitoring: TrueNAS and Unraid have built-in SMART monitoring dashboards with email alerts on drive errors. Proxmox installs smartmontools by default; smartd is enabled and checks supported disks every 30 minutes, emailing root when it detects errors or warnings. Its web UI can show per-disk SMART values, but it lacks a NAS-oriented health dashboard.
 Drive spin-down: Unraid's per-drive spin-down is a home NAS feature with no Proxmox equivalent. All drives attached to Proxmox spin continuously unless you configure hdparm or sdparm manually and schedule it.
 Power efficiency: Proxmox is not optimised for low-power idle states. Idle power varies with hardware, active services, storage activity and disk power-management settings; spinning down idle hard drives can reduce consumption where the configuration supports it.
 Consumer-friendly management: Every storage management task on Proxmox requires either the web UI (for VM-level operations) or SSH CLI work. TrueNAS and Unraid provide GUIs for share creation, user management, and quota setting.
 When Proxmox Is the Right Choice
 Proxmox makes sense for home NAS-adjacent use when your primary workload is virtual machines or containers and storage is secondary. If you are running a Windows VM for gaming, a development environment, a home server running multiple services in isolation, and you want all of that on one physical machine with storage available, Proxmox is a reasonable choice.
 Proxmox also makes sense if you want to experiment with enterprise-grade technology for learning purposes. The HA clustering, live migration, and Ceph storage integration in Proxmox are technologies used in production data centres. Running them at home provides genuine learning value that translates to professional skills.
 Proxmox is not the right choice if you want a straightforward home NAS for media storage and file sharing, or if you are new to Linux and want a managed experience. Start with TrueNAS Scale or Unraid for those use cases. Both have clear upgrade paths to Proxmox-based setups if your needs grow.

 Australian hardware note: A common approach is to pass an HBA or storage controller through to the TrueNAS VM, but TrueNAS also documents passing individual hardware disks; controller passthrough requires VT-d or AMD-Vi. LSI 9207-8i, 9211-8i, and similar cards (flashed to IT mode) are available used on eBay AU. These are the standard recommendation across the homelab community for ZFS passthrough because they expose drives directly without a RAID layer. Verify the card is in IT mode (not IR mode) before purchasing; IR mode adds a hardware RAID layer that interferes with ZFS.

 Can Proxmox replace TrueNAS entirely? 
 For a technical user comfortable with Linux administration, yes. You can share ZFS datasets via Samba, configure SMART monitoring, set up snapshot tasks via cron, and manage everything through the CLI. You lose TrueNAS's GUI for these tasks, but the underlying functionality is equivalent. 
 Does Proxmox support ZFS RAIDZ? 
 Yes. Proxmox has native ZFS support and can create mirror, RAIDZ1, RAIDZ2, and RAIDZ3 pools during installation or via the web UI post-install. These use OpenZFS RAIDZ layouts, but available features, defaults and management behavior can differ by OpenZFS version and platform integration. The difference is management: Proxmox has a basic ZFS management interface in the web UI, while TrueNAS provides a more comprehensive NAS-oriented GUI for pool monitoring, scrubs, and snapshots.
 Is Proxmox free? 
 Yes. Proxmox VE is open source and free to use without a subscription. The Proxmox enterprise repository requires a paid subscription and provides more heavily tested packages for production use; the free no-subscription repository has the same features and generally receives package updates earlier, with less validation. Home homelab builders use the no-subscription repository without any functional limitation. A pop-up at login reminds you of the subscription status but does not affect any features.
 How much RAM does Proxmox need to run alongside TrueNAS? 
 Budget RAM for both systems independently. Proxmox overhead is minimal (1-2GB), but each VM and LXC container needs its own RAM allocation. TrueNAS requires at least 8GB RAM for basic operation, while additional memory depends on drive count, clients and enabled services. Proxmox requires memory for its OS and services plus each guest, so total host RAM should be sized for the actual storage and virtual-machine workloads.
 Can Proxmox run Unraid as a VM? 
 Unraid 7.3 and later supports internal boot and TPM-based licensing, and Unraid's official installer is intended for Proxmox and other compatible virtual environments. Some homelab builders have done it, but it is unsupported, may break on Unraid updates, and defeats the advantage of Unraid's hardware flexibility. If you want Proxmox plus NAS, run TrueNAS inside Proxmox rather than Unraid.

How much RAM does a NAS or homelab server need?
How much RAM for TrueNAS, Proxmox, Unraid or a Synology

By Harry Saarinen · Updated November 2, 2026

BROWSE LISTINGS
DDR4 ECC memory for NAS and server builds
DDR4 SO-DIMMs without ECC (Celeron Synology units)
Registered DDR4 for used servers
HPE MicroServer Gen10 Plus v2 memory
AMD Ryzen Embedded V1500B memory support
DDR4 desktop memory, for an old PC turned NAS
Memory prices over time
IN THIS GUIDE
The whole answer, by platform
The checklist
How the number adds up
TrueNAS: 8 GB for eight drives, then the workload
Proxmox VE: 2 GB, every guest, and a cache you size yourself
Unraid: an OS that lives in RAM and a 20 percent ZFS cache
Synology: a ceiling per model and a warranty clause
ZFS on any platform: the ARC, deduplication and L2ARC
ECC on a NAS: what each vendor says
What the apps ask for
Four builds added up line by line
Which processors and machines take which memory
The rules that are folklore, and where each came from
What each tier costs
How to see what your system is really using
What to do with this on a listing page

A NAS that only stores and shares files is well served by 8 GB on TrueNAS or Unraid and, on a Synology, by the 2 to 8 GB it ships with; a few apps take it to 16 GB, and each virtual machine adds its full memory on top. Proxmox VE is a hypervisor first: 2 GB for itself, the sum of what its guests are given, and a ZFS cache that a fresh install caps at 10 percent of RAM. The rule most forums still quote, 1 GB of RAM per TB of storage, traces to the FreeNAS 8 documentation wiki, archived in 2012, and appears in no current TrueNAS or OpenZFS document; iXsystems’ own TrueNAS Mini R ships with 32 GB for up to 216 TB of raw storage.

The whole answer, by platform

The vendor figures carry their version; the three middle columns are this guide’s tiers. Each row links the section that argues for it.

PLATFORM, OCTOBER 15, 2026	WHAT THE VENDOR PUBLISHES	FILES ONLY	A FEW APPS	WITH VMS	WHAT MOVES IT UP
TrueNAS Community Edition 25.10 (TrueNAS)	8 GB up to eight drives, then 1 GB per drive after that	8 GB	16 GB	16 GB plus each VM	serving iSCSI to other hosts (16 GB good, 32 GB or more optimal), Active Directory (+2 GB), deduplication
Proxmox VE 9.2 (Proxmox)	2 GB plus guests plus about 1 GB per TB of used ZFS or Ceph storage	8 GB with ZFS	16 GB	2 GB + guests + ZFS cache + 1 GB free	the ARC budget, Ceph at 8 GiB per OSD, passthrough VMs
Unraid 7.3 (Unraid)	no OS minimum since 2025; VMs 8 GB minimum, 16 GB or more recommended	8 GB	16 GB	16 GB plus each running VM	a ZFS pool, machine-learning apps
Synology DSM 7.4 (Synology)	a ceiling per model: 6, 8 or 32 GB; the RS422+ fixed at 2 GB	the 2 to 8 GB it ships with	6 or 8 GB on Celeron models, 8 to 16 GB on Ryzen	16 to 32 GB on Ryzen; Celeron models stop at 6 or 8 GB (two to four small VMs)	Photos, Virtual Machine Manager, backups, SSD cache
Proxmox Backup Server 4.2 (PBS)	4 GiB plus 1 GiB per TiB of datastore	4 GiB + 1 GiB per TiB (24 GiB for 20 TiB)	-	-	datastore size
Linux with OpenZFS 2.4 (ZFS)	“8GB+ of memory for the best performance”	8 GB	16 GB	8 GB plus guests	deduplication, L2ARC

The tiers rest on the vendors’ figures, the 16 and 32 GB in iXsystems’ TrueNAS Minis and the apps’ own figures. iXsystems’ 16 and 32 GB for VMs describe a TrueNAS box serving iSCSI storage to VMs on other hosts; a VM running on TrueNAS itself is counted at its own size. What decides the purchase is a sum - the platform’s base, every VM at its full size, each app, a cache budget if the pool is ZFS - and two limits above it: the box’s maximum, which on a Synology is 6, 8 or 32 GB by model (the RS422+ is fixed at 2 GB), and the price of the module type it takes. The column you need is set by the virtual machines you run, not by the size of the pool.

The checklist
Write the sum before you open a listing: base, every VM at full size, each app, a cache budget, headroom (the terms, four builds).
Find the box’s ceiling first. It is the box maker’s figure: HPE caps the MicroServer Gen10 Plus at 32 GB though its Xeon E-2224 addresses 128 GB (the tables).
Match the module type: SO-DIMM or full-size, unbuffered or registered, ECC or not; a Ryzen Synology takes ECC SO-DIMMs. Registered vs unbuffered has the rules.
Count every VM at its full allocation. Ballooning guarantees only a minimum, and a passthrough VM cannot balloon on Proxmox or Unraid.
Count nothing for swap or KSM. TrueNAS removed swap management in 24.10, and Proxmox’s KSM starts merging only when memory is nearly committed.
Set the ZFS cache on purpose; each platform’s default is in the ARC table.
Leave deduplication off unless zdb -S simulates a ratio comfortably above 2x (deduplication).
Buy RAM before an L2ARC. Each block it caches costs 96 bytes of ARC.
Fill a Synology in matched pairs, with the warranty clause in view (upgrading a Synology).
Test new memory, then read “used” correctly: a full graph on a NAS is cache (how to see it).
How the number adds up

Every platform here is sized by the same five terms, and vendors publish only the first, which is why their minimums look small. Desktops, workstations and local AI are sized in how much RAM do you need.

The platform base is small

TrueNAS’s 8 GB covers the system and ZFS for up to eight drives; Proxmox VE asks 2 GB; Unraid publishes no figure; Synology’s DSM keeps 1.5 GB of an 8 GB unit when it hosts VMs, and 10 percent from 16 GB up. These are floors, not purchase figures.

Virtual machines are counted whole

TrueNAS’s 25.10 documentation: “While a VM is running, these resources are not available to the host computer or other VMs.” Proxmox VE guarantees a ballooned VM only its minimum, so a host sized to the minimums makes guests swap when they reach for the rest, and a VM with a PCIe or GPU passthrough device cannot balloon at all. Overhead comes on top. Proxmox’s 9.0 release notes say VMs “usually consume a higher amount of memory on the host than the amount that is reported from inside the guest”, with no figure; Synology publishes one, 128 MB per VM plus 80 MB per virtual CPU and 32 MB per virtual disk.

Apps and containers are limits, not reservations

TrueNAS’s Apps catalog gives apps such as Plex, Jellyfin and Immich a 4096 MB memory limit by default; Docker Engine and Unraid’s Docker set none; a Proxmox LXC container defaults to 512 MiB. A cap overstates what a quiet machine uses; with no cap, Docker warns, a host that runs out lets the kernel’s out-of-memory killer take any process.

The cache takes what is left

On ZFS the read cache is the ARC, and each platform sets how much of the remainder it may take (the ARC table). XFS and Btrfs disks in an Unraid array, and a Synology volume, use the ordinary page cache, the subject of RAM caching.

Headroom, because swap will not save you

TrueNAS 24.10 removed swap management, and a TrueNAS staff member wrote on May 4, 2024: “We do not recommend using a SWAP drive. ZFS expects ARC to be in RAM.” Proxmox warns that swap on a ZFS zvol can block the server and advises leaving 1 GB free for the host. Treat RAM as a hard budget and leave room above the sum.

TrueNAS: 8 GB for eight drives, then the workload

As of October 15, 2026, iXsystems recommends TrueNAS Community Edition 25.10.7, from September 2, 2026, for general users. TrueNAS 27, renamed from 26, is at its first release candidate (October 6, 2026), for early adopters, with OpenZFS 2.4. TrueNAS CORE ended with 13.3-U1.2 on April 29, 2025, and iXsystems names 25.10 as its migration path.

The sizing rule in the hardware guide

The 25.10 hardware guide’s minimum is a 2-core x86-64 processor, 8 GB of memory and a 16 GB boot SSD; the installation page says “TrueNAS requires at least 8GB of RAM (more is better) and a 20GB Boot Device.” The TrueNAS 27 guide keeps 8 GB with “at least” added. The rule that scales it has been the same from 22.12 through 27 and in CORE 13: “You should have 8 GB of RAM for basic TrueNAS operations with up to eight drives. … Add 1 GB for each drive added after eight to benefit most use cases.” It counts drives, not terabytes: a 12-drive box starts at 12 GB, a 24-bay chassis at 24 GB, before any app or VM. It first appeared in the FreeNAS 11.3 guide.

Then the guide names what actually moves the figure: “A 20 TB pool backing many high-performance VMs over iSCSI might need more RAM than a 200 TB pool storing archival data.” For a box that backs VMs on other hosts over iSCSI it asks for at least 16 GB, with 32 GB or more for optimal performance, and it adds 2 GB for Active Directory through Winbind, more for each app and VM it runs itself, 5 GB per TB of deduplicated storage and about 1 GB per 50 GB of L2ARC.

Apps, containers and virtual machines

TrueNAS 24.10 moved Apps from Kubernetes to Docker, claiming faster deployment and lower idle CPU but nothing about memory. The catalog’s Plex, Jellyfin and Immich apps default to a 4096 MB memory limit. One mismatch is worth fixing: Immich asks for at least 6 GB, and its FAQ warns that “memory constraints work by terminating the container”, so if Immich’s machine-learning jobs die, raise its limit first.

The 25.10 VM tutorial sets a 256 MiB minimum per VM, offers minimum and maximum memory for ballooning, and warns that a VM given all available memory “can slow the host system or prevent other VMs from starting”. An iXsystems engineer wrote in August 2022 that the middleware lowered the ARC’s maximum when VMs were configured, and 25.04 and 25.10 list fixes for the ARC not giving memory back fast enough to VMs (NAS-135904, NAS-135499): run a current release on a box that mixes a large cache with VMs. LXC containers, new in 25.04, can run without a limit, and “Memory allocated to containers reduces available memory for TrueNAS ZFS caching.”

The cache took half before 24.04 and nearly all of it since

Until TrueNAS SCALE 24.04 the ARC stopped at half of RAM, the OpenZFS Linux default. The 24.04 “Dragonfish” notes record the change: “ZFS ARC memory allocations are updated and behave identically to TrueNAS CORE.” With kernel 6.6’s Multi-Gen LRU code, the larger ARC caused swap thrash on 24.04.0, and 24.04.1 (May 28, 2024) disabled swap and Multi-Gen LRU. TrueNAS 25.04 moved to OpenZFS 2.3, whose ceiling is the larger of memory minus 1 GiB and five-eighths of it. On a 64 GB TrueNAS box the ARC may grow to about 63 GiB, where SCALE before 24.04 stopped it at 32 GiB, so extra RAM is no longer half wasted, and advice from 2023 or earlier to raise zfs_arc_max by hand is out of date.

What iXsystems puts in its own boxes

Every current TrueNAS Mini ships with ECC DDR4: the Mini X with 16 GB (to 32 GB, for up to 90 TB raw), the Mini X+ with 32 GB (to 64 GB, 105 TB) and the Mini R with 32 GB (to 64 GB, 216 TB); the Mini X fills its four slots in same-capacity pairs. The R20 manual gives 32 to 192 GB against up to 2.9 PB raw with expansion: by this guide’s arithmetic about 0.15 GB per raw TB in the Mini R and 0.07 in a full R20. iXsystems does not follow the per-terabyte rule in its own hardware. The disks are the drive site’s drives for a NAS guide.

Proxmox VE: 2 GB, every guest, and a cache you size yourself

Proxmox VE 9.2 was released on May 21, 2026, and this section follows its documentation version 9.2.13 of September 24, 2026; Proxmox VE 8 reached end of life in August 2026. The installation chapter’s minimum, 1 GB plus guest RAM, is labeled for evaluation only. The recommendation is “Minimum 2 GB for the OS and Proxmox VE services, plus designated memory for guests. For Ceph and ZFS, additional memory is required; approximately 1GB of memory for every TB of used storage.”

Four formulas from one vendor

Proxmox is the one vendor here whose general rule is still per terabyte, and its documents give four formulas, to be quoted rather than merged:

WHERE IT APPEARS	WHAT IT SAYS
Installation chapter and requirements page	about 1 GB per TB of used storage, for ZFS or Ceph
Installation chapter, “ZFS Performance Tips”	4 GB plus 1 GB per TB of raw disk
Administration guide, “Limit ZFS Memory Usage”	an ARC of at least 2 GiB plus 1 GiB per TiB of available storage: 10 GiB for an 8 TiB pool
Administration guide, ZFS hardware	“at least 8GB to start. In practice, use as much as you can get”

For a mirror of two 8 TB drives holding 5 TB, the four give: 7 GB (the 2 GB base plus 5 GB for the used terabytes), 20 GB (4 GB plus 16 TB raw), an ARC of 9.3 GiB (2 GiB plus 7.3 TiB available) and at least 8 GB. The ARC rule is the one to buy with, because it budgets one line of the sum rather than the whole machine.

The 10 percent cap

Ballooning, KSM and containers

Ballooning hands extra memory to a VM only while host usage is under a target, 80 percent by default; under pressure the guest swaps and, in the last resort, runs its own out-of-memory killer. Proxmox does not recommend the Windows balloon driver on critical systems. Kernel Samepage Merging is on by default, Proxmox warns it exposes VMs to side-channel attacks, and by a reading of Proxmox’s ksmtuned script it only starts merging near 80 percent of RAM committed. Buy for each VM’s full allocation. Ballooning guarantees only the minimum, and a passthrough VM always holds all of its memory.

An LXC container shares the host kernel, its memory a cgroup limit; Proxmox calls containers lightweight but publishes no saving. One app maker steers the other way: Immich “runs well” in “a full virtual machine” and says Docker in LXC “is not recommended”, so budget Immich on Proxmox as a VM.

Unraid: an OS that lives in RAM and a 20 percent ZFS cache

There is no published minimum

That page now redirects, and no current page states an OS minimum; the “4 GB” on unraid.net’s getting-started list is the size of the USB drive. The ARC ceiling, release by release

With zfs_arc_max at 0, OpenZFS 2.3 and 2.4 cap the ARC at the larger of memory minus 1 GiB and five-eighths of memory, which above about 2.7 GiB is memory minus 1 GiB. The 2.2 branch, still maintained, keeps the old Linux default of half.

OpenZFS 2.3 and 2.4; TrueNAS 24.04 and later	memory minus 1 GiB	31 GiB	63 GiB
Proxmox VE, installed with 8.1 or later	10 percent, at most 16 GiB	3.2 GiB	6.4 GiB
Proxmox Backup Server on ZFS	50 percent	16 GiB	32 GiB
Unraid 6.12 to 7.2	one eighth	4 GiB	8 GiB
Unraid 7.3	20 percent	6.4 GiB	12.8 GiB

The ceiling is not a reservation: the ARC gives memory back under pressure down to a floor of 1/32 of memory, and lowering zfs_arc_max on a running system does not shrink it until there is pressure (RAM caching has the mechanics). A large ARC is not a leak; an ARC capped far below the working set is a choice that costs disk reads. One OpenZFS page has not caught up: Workload Tuning still says “half of system memory on Linux”.

Deduplication is the one per-terabyte rule

Deduplication keeps a table of every unique block, and the table must sit in RAM to be fast. The published figures disagree:
